models_evaluated: Four open-weight small language models (1.2B, 4.3B, 7.6B, 9.2B parameters) run locally via Ollama

links.outcome: Paired accuracy change when models were offered a prompted abstention option (deferral)
links.effect: Only the 1.2B model had a paired effect distinguishable from noise, and it was negative (-6.7 points, 95% CI [-12.7,-0.7]). The 7.6B model's effect reversed from a naive +0.8 to -5.3 points (95% CI [-9.3,-1.3]); 8 of 12 abstentions forfeited correct answers.
links.quote: a prompted abstention option is not a free safety improvement for any of the four models once evaluated with paired, coverage-aware statistics rather than naive answered-item accuracy.

links.outcome: Calibration and error-detection quality of verbalized confidence (AUROC, ECE)
links.effect: Verbalized confidence AUROC 0.490-0.645 (4.3B indistinguishable from chance); ECE 0.148-0.378 versus 0.041-0.141 reported for proprietary frontier models on the same benchmark family.
links.quote: Verbalized condence remains poorly informative about correctness as a ranking signal (AUROC 0.4900.645; one model, the 4.3B, is statistically indistin- guishable from chance) and severely miscalibrated in the aggregate sense (ECE 0.1480.378, well above the 0.0410.141 range Boie et al. report for proprietary frontier models on the same under- lying benchmark family).

screen.reason: Evaluates small open-weight LLMs on psychiatric medical questions, specifically testing whether adding a prompted abstention option acts as a reliable safety mechanism / guardrail against errors.
